Q: Making Composer consider other directories for packages, to avoid duplication A:

Composer is generally designed around a single dependency tree per project, so what you're trying to do fights its normal workflow a bit.

The cleanest approach is usually to treat core_module as the main Composer project and install gateway packages there, rather than letting every plugin maintain its own isolated vendor/ directory.

Something like this:

{
    "config": {
        "vendor-dir": "../core_module/vendor"
    }
}

in the gateway plugins will probably work to some extent, since Composer should detect already-installed packages and avoid downloading duplicate copies unnecessarily.

That said, sharing a vendor directory across multiple sibling packages can get messy over time:

  • removing one plugin may leave unused packages behind

  • dependency version conflicts become harder to reason about

  • plugins stop being fully self-contained

Personally, I'd probably go with one of these approaches instead:

  1. Single shared Composer root
    Have one top-level Composer project that manages all dependencies centrally. This is how Composer is intended to be used.

  2. Path repositories + symlinks
    Useful during development, though Windows support can sometimes be annoying depending on environment/setup.

  3. Accept some duplication
    Disk space is usually cheaper than maintenance complexity nowadays, and isolated plugins are easier to add/remove cleanly.

I don't think Composer has a built-in concept of:

"this package already exists in another sibling plugin's vendor directory"

because dependency resolution is normally project-scoped, not plugin-scoped.

So your shared vendor-dir idea is probably the closest thing to what you want, even if it isn't perfectly compartmentalized.

Q: Distribute content instead of distribute app in xcode 10.1 A:

If you develop a Unity app on Windows and transfer the build folder to a Mac through Google Drive, this may be the cause of the issue.

During the transfer, Google Drive scans the files and may automatically change the extensions of files that contain XML content but do not already have an .xml extension. This can affect your LaunchScreen-storyboard files, which Google Drive renames with an XML extension. As a result, when you open the project on a Mac using Xcode, Xcode assumes the LaunchScreen files are missing.

Although the build itself succeeds, Xcode may interpret the project as something intended for developer sharing rather than app distribution, which can cause the “Distribute App” button to appear as “Distribute Content” instead.

If your setup matches this situation, simply zip the build folder before transferring it to the Mac you use for app distribution.

Q: How to set dynamic meta tags in a React SPA so they are visible to search engine crawlers? A:

React Helmet is fine if all you care about is updating the browser tab title, but I would not rely on it as the core SEO solution.

Google does render JavaScript now, so Helmet can work for Google in a lot of cases. The bigger issue is that many crawlers, preview bots, and AI search systems still look at the initial HTML response first. Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Bing, and various AI crawlers are not guaranteed to wait for your React app to fully load and inject meta tags.

The safer approach is making sure the final meta tags are already in the HTML returned from the server.

For pages you already know ahead of time like blogs, docs, landing pages, product pages, or marketing content, prerendering or static generation is usually the best option. If you are open to switching frameworks, Next.js is probably the cleanest long term solution because each route can generate its own metadata before the page is even sent to the browser.

For truly dynamic content, SSR or ISR is the better route using something like Next.js, Remix, or Vike.

React Helmet still has value, but I would not treat it as a complete SEO strategy if search visibility and social previews actually matter. The real test is checking view source, not just Inspect Element. If your title, description, canonical tags, Open Graph tags, and structured data are visible in the raw HTML response, crawlers are much more likely to index them correctly.

Q: Stored procedure in MySQL after run for unknown reason returns query interrupted A:

In stored objects, when you use a local variable name which is duplicated by the a column of the same name in the table then the name only is always treated as a variable whereas the name accompanied with the table alias is treated as the column name.

Look at your code:

CREATE DEFINER=`sparkle`@`%` PROCEDURE `finish_repetition`(
  IN devotion_id INT, 
...
)
BEGIN
... 
    SELECT 
...
    FROM 
      repetitions
    WHERE 
      devotion_id = devotion_id 
...
END

In your WHERE you compare two copies of the variable which produces either TRUE or NULL and never prodices FALSE.

You must use

...
    FROM 
      repetitions
    WHERE 
      devotion_id = repetitions.devotion_id 
...

In this case devotion_id is a variable value, and repetitions.devotion_id is a column value.

But the best practice is to avoid name duplication. Instead use in_devotion_id instead of devotion_id, for example.
